chapter_title: Program Structure and Memory in Embedded Systems

screens.title: Program Structure and Memory
screens.subtitle: How startup code, runtime memory regions, and variable scopes shape reliable embedded programs

narration.text: When a microcontroller powers up it does not start in your main function. Instead, execution follows the reset vector into vendor-provided startup code that prepares R A M, sets the stack pointer, and then transfers control to your program. Understanding this startup sequence and the memory layout that follows — code in flash, initialized data copied into R A M, zeroed BSS, a limited stack, and an optional heap — is essential for writing robust embedded software. In this lesson we will see why local arrays can crash a system, why globals persist forever, and why dynamic allocation is usually avoided on tiny microcontrollers. You will learn where variables live, how the main infinite loop fits into a larger runtime, and the concrete debugging techniques to inspect addresses and spot overflows. By the end you will be able to predict where a variable appears in memory, explain the risk of deep recursion, and choose allocation strategies that keep systems predictable. Think about a device that must run unattended for years — which memory choices keep it safe?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Startup code + memory layout determine where variables live and how safe your embedded program will be.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the startup sequence that runs before your main function, explain how flash and R A M are used for code and data, and identify where globals, locals, and static variables are stored. You will practice reasoning about limited stack size and why deep recursion or large local arrays can cause stack overflow. You will also be able to state why dynamic allocation is risky on small microcontrollers and propose static, deterministic alternatives. Each objective ties to real tasks: inspecting addresses with a debugger, choosing storage for configuration data, and designing a main loop that keeps stack usage small. These skills matter because embedded systems often run without supervision and have tiny R A M budgets, so predictable memory use is essential for reliability. As you study the examples, try to predict addresses for variables and test those predictions with a debugger. That habit moves understanding from abstract to practical.

screens.title: Startup Code and the Reset Vector
screens.subtitle: What runs before main and why initialization matters

narration.text: When a microcontroller resets, execution begins at a fixed address called the reset vector. That vector points to startup code supplied by the compiler or chip vendor. The startup code performs critical setup before your application runs. It sets the processor stack pointer to a known R A M location so function calls and local variables work predictably. It copies initialized global data from flash into R A M so variables with initial values are ready to use. It zeroes the BSS region so uninitialized globals and static variables start at zero. Finally, it calls the main function. This sequence is not optional: if the stack pointer is wrong or the data copy is skipped, functions can return to invalid addresses or globals will contain garbage. A concrete example is a peripheral driver that reads a configuration variable initialized in. data; if startup code fails to copy. data into R A M, that configuration will be incorrect and the driver may misconfigure hardware. A common misconception is that main is where execution starts; in fact main is an application entry point called after system initialization. Key takeaway: the startup phase enforces runtime invariants — stack pointer, correct global values, and a predictable environment for main. When debugging early boot failures, inspect the reset vector, the stack pointer, and whether. data and. bss were set as expected.

keyIdea.title: Why startup matters
keyIdea.text: Startup code ensures the CPU, stack, and data sections are ready so main can run with predictable state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Startup Code and Reset Vector
Core Concept

Startup sequence

A numbered process shows the tasks the startup code performs before calling main.

1. Reset vector transfer
CPU jumps to a fixed vector which points at the startup routine.
2. Stack pointer setup
Initialize SP to a high RAM address so stack grows downward safely.
3. Data & BSS init
Copy .data from flash to RAM and zero .bss for uninitialized globals.
4. Call main
Transfer control to your application entry point once runtime is ready.
Key Takeaway

Early initialization is required for predictable program behavior; failures here cause hard faults or corrupted globals.

Concrete example
Driver config example

If a peripheral driver reads a global configuration in .data but the startup copy from flash fails, the driver sees garbage and may enable the wrong pins, causing hardware misbehavior.

Common misconception

Many assume main is the first code executed. In embedded systems, main is called after startup completes important runtime setup.

Check your understanding
  • What happens if the stack pointer is left uninitialized?
  • Why must .data be copied from flash?

screens.title: Memory Layout: .text, .data, .bss
screens.subtitle: Roles of flash and RAM in storing code and data

narration.text: Embedded memory is partitioned so each kind of program content lives where it is safe and efficient. The code region, often called. text, contains the machine instructions and is stored in flash because flash retains code across power cycles and is read-only at run time. The. data region holds global and static variables that have explicit initial values; their initial values are stored in flash and then copied into R A M during startup. The BSS region contains global and static variables that are implicitly zero-initialized. They occupy R A M but do not need initial values in flash; startup code zeroes that area. The stack is a R A M region used for local variables, function parameters, and return addresses. It typically grows downward from a high address. The heap is another R A M region reserved for dynamic allocation; on small systems it is often omitted or discouraged. A concrete example: a global lookup table defined with initial values will be listed in. data and will consume flash space for its initializer plus R A M at runtime. A large local array declared inside a function uses stack space only while the function executes. The main misconception to avoid is thinking R A M and flash are interchangeable; flash is slower and write-limited, R A M is volatile and much more limited in size. Key takeaway: pick storage locations intentionally — constants and code in flash, persistent runtime variables in. data or. bss, and transient buffers on the stack with care.

keyIdea.title: Memory regions
keyIdea.text: .text in flash; .data and .bss in RAM; stack for locals; heap for dynamic allocation — each has different lifetime and constraints.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Memory Layout: .text, .data, .bss
Definition

Regions and responsibilities

Cards below describe each region, how data arrives there, and lifetimes.

.text — code in flash
Machine instructions live in flash; read-only at runtime and persistent across resets.
.data — initialized globals
Initial values stored in flash are copied to RAM at startup so globals have expected values.
.bss — zeroed globals
Uninitialized globals and static variables are zeroed into RAM by startup code.
Practical example
Global lookup table

A table declared with initializers uses flash for the constants and RAM for the active table if you need to modify it at runtime. If you never modify it, mark it const so it can remain only in flash.

Misconception check

Do not assume flash behaves like RAM. Writes to flash are slower, require erase cycles, and are limited compared to RAM.

Key Takeaway

Choose flash for code and immutable data; use RAM for variables that must change at runtime and control stack usage for temporary storage.

screens.title: Program Structure: main and the Infinite Loop
screens.subtitle: Initialization, main tasks, and the perpetual run loop

narration.text: An embedded program typically follows a clear pattern: run initialization once, then enter a perpetual main loop that performs input processing, state updates, and output. The code you write usually looks like an init section that sets up peripherals and global state, followed by a while loop that runs forever. This structure keeps C P U use predictable, especially on bare-metal systems without an operating system. A concrete example: initialize GPIO and timers in an init function, then in each loop iteration read switches, debounce inputs, update control state, and write LED outputs. That loop must be designed with stack and timing in mind: avoid deep call chains and large temporary buffers inside the loop to limit stack usage. Interrupt handlers should be brief and avoid heavy stack use themselves. A misconception is to treat the main loop like a threaded scheduler; without an OS, long blocking calls can prevent other periodic tasks from running. Favor short, deterministic functions called in the loop or use hardware timers and flags to coordinate work. Consider worst-case stack usage across both the loop and interrupt contexts when sizing the stack. Key takeaway: structure your program so initialization is separate, the main loop is short and predictable, and stack usage is bounded at all times.

keyIdea.title: Loop discipline
keyIdea.text: Keep initialization distinct from a short, deterministic main loop and bound stack usage for reliability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Program Structure: main and the Infinite Loop
Process Flow

Init → Main loop

A code example card shows the canonical pattern; the narration explains runtime constraints.

// Global variables
uint32_t g_systemState = 0;

void init_hardware(void);
void process_input(void);
void update_output(void);

int main(void) {
  init_hardware();
  while (1) {
    process_input();
    update_output();
  }
}
Analogy

Think of init as setup before opening a shop, and the main loop as serving customers repeatedly — it must remain responsive.

Key Takeaway

Design the main loop to be short, avoid large local buffers, and coordinate longer work with flags or timers.

Concrete scenario
Debounce and update

In each loop pass, sample inputs, debounce with a small state machine, update the global state, and write outputs. Keep each function short to limit stack depth.

Misconception check

Do not use long blocking delays inside the loop unless you understand their impact on periodic tasks and interrupts.

screens.title: Variable Storage Classes: Global, Local, Static
screens.subtitle: Lifetime and scope explained with examples

narration.text: Variables in C have storage duration and scope that determine where and how long they exist. Global variables are declared outside any function and persist for the entire program lifetime. They typically live in. data if initialized or. bss if zero-initialized. Use globals when data truly must be shared across modules, but be mindful of potential name collisions and harder reasoning about state. Local variables are declared inside functions and are stored on the stack; they exist only while the function executes and are reclaimed when the function returns. Large local arrays increase stack usage and can cause stack overflow if the stack is small. Static variables declared inside a function retain their value between calls but are limited in scope to the function; they live in the data or bss region rather than on the stack. A concrete example: a static counter inside a function that records how many times the function has been called persists across calls without exposing the counter globally. A common misconception is that static equals local lifetime; static changes storage duration to program lifetime while keeping scope limited. Key takeaway: choose globals for application-wide persistent data, locals for transient working storage, and static for per-function persistent state without external visibility. When in doubt, prefer scoped static variables over public globals for encapsulation.

keyIdea.title: Storage choices
keyIdea.text: Global: program lifetime and shared; Local: stack-lifetime; Static: program lifetime with limited scope.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Variable Storage Classes
Definition

Global, Local, Static

Cards below explain lifetime and scope with a concrete usage note for embedded systems.

Global
Declared outside functions, accessible across files with extern, and exist for the program lifetime.
Local (stack)
Allocated on the stack, exist only during function execution; be careful with size and recursion.
Static inside function
Has program lifetime like a global but scope limited to the function, stored in .data/.bss.
Key Takeaway

Use static for per-function persistence, avoid excessive global state, and keep locals small to protect the stack.

Concrete example
Static counter

A static counter inside a function increments each call and persists without exposing the variable globally. It occupies .data or .bss, not the stack.

Misconception check

Static limits scope but does not limit lifetime — it lives for the whole program run, unlike locals.

screens.title: Stack Behavior and Stack Overflow
screens.subtitle: How the stack grows, what consumes it, and why overflow happens

narration.text: The stack is a region of R A M used for function frames: local variables, parameters, and return addresses. In many microcontrollers the stack grows downward from a high address toward lower addresses. Each function call pushes a new frame, and each return pops it. Large local arrays, many nested calls, or deep recursion increase stack depth and can exhaust the available stack region. When the stack pointer moves past its configured limit, it overwrites adjacent memory — often corrupting global variables, the heap, or other critical state — and typically leads to a hard fault or system crash. A concrete example: declaring a local array of one thousand 32-bit integers on a system with only a few kilobytes of R A M will likely overflow the stack. A common mistake is assuming the desktop behavior applies: microcontrollers may have only a small stack, so avoid large automatic arrays and deep recursion. Practical strategies include: make large buffers global or static so they occupy. data or. bss instead of the stack, check compiler-generated stack estimates if available, and keep interrupt handlers short to reduce combined worst-case stack usage. Key takeaway: treat stack as a scarce resource and design functions to use small, bounded local storage.

keyIdea.title: Stack safety
keyIdea.text: Stack frames grow with calls; limit local sizes and recursion to prevent stack overflow and memory corruption.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Stack Behavior and Stack Overflow
Definition

Stack growth and frames

A vertical stack of call frames uses RAM; callers and callees add to depth. Keep frames small.

What consumes stack
Local arrays, saved registers, return addresses, and parameter passing.
Symptoms of overflow
Corrupted globals, strange behavior, and hard faults at return or interrupt boundaries.
Prevention
Use static buffers for big data, avoid deep recursion, estimate worst-case usage.
Key Takeaway

Design to bound stack use: move large buffers out of locals and keep call depth predictable.

Concrete example
Local bigArray pitfall

Declaring uint32_t bigArray[1000]; as a local on a microcontroller with 2 KB RAM will likely overflow the stack and crash the program. Make it global or static instead.

Misconception check

Embedded stacks are tiny compared to desktops; desktop habits like large automatic buffers are unsafe here.

screens.title: Heap and Dynamic Allocation
screens.subtitle: Why malloc is discouraged in bare-metal embedded systems

narration.text: Dynamic memory allocation gives flexibility on systems with abundant R A M, but on microcontrollers it introduces unpredictability. The heap lives in R A M and grows or shrinks when you call allocation functions. Over time, a sequence of allocations and frees can fragment the heap so free blocks are available but not contiguous, preventing future allocations even though total free memory seems sufficient. On small systems with a tiny heap, fragmentation, allocation failures, and the difficulty of handling allocation errors make malloc a risky choice. Embedded best practice is to avoid heap usage by preallocating fixed-size buffers, using static pools, or employing simple slab allocators with deterministic behavior. A concrete example: using malloc to receive network packets of variable sizes can fragment memory heavily; instead, allocate a pool of maximum-sized packet buffers at startup and reuse them. A common misconception is that avoiding heap means losing flexibility; in fact, a well-designed static pool plus clear ownership rules delivers both predictability and sufficient flexibility. Key takeaway: prefer deterministic allocation strategies over dynamic allocation on small microcontrollers, and plan for allocation failures if you must use the heap.

keyIdea.title: Heap caution
keyIdea.text: Heap fragmentation and allocation failure make malloc unsuitable for many embedded systems; prefer static pools or fixed buffers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Heap and Dynamic Allocation
Comparison

Heap vs static allocation

Compare risks and benefits and see practical alternatives to malloc.

Heap (malloc)
Flexible, but risks fragmentation and unpredictable failures on small RAM.
Static pools / globals
Deterministic, predictable memory use, and easier to reason about for long-running devices.
Key Takeaway

Choose deterministic allocation strategies in embedded systems; reserve heap for noncritical, well-tested subsystems only.

Concrete scenario
Packet buffer pool

Instead of malloc per packet, reserve a fixed pool of buffers and hand them out and reclaim them deterministically to prevent fragmentation.

Misconception check

Avoid assuming heap errors are rare; on constrained devices a single leak or fragmentation pattern can eventually starve the system.

screens.title: Common Memory Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.subtitle: Buffer overflow, uninitialized pointers, dangling pointers, and memory leaks

narration.text: Several recurring memory mistakes cause crashes and undefined behavior on microcontrollers. Buffer overflow happens when code writes past an array boundary and corrupts adjacent memory; this often occurs with incorrect loop bounds or unchecked input. Stack overflow results from excessive local allocation or deep recursion. An uninitialized pointer used as if it points to valid memory causes unpredictable behavior or hard faults because the pointer may reference an invalid address. A dangling pointer refers to memory that has been freed or gone out of scope; accessing it yields undefined results. Memory leaks arise when dynamic allocations are not freed, eventually exhausting heap space. To prevent these mistakes, follow concrete defensive practices: use bounds-checked access functions, prefer fixed-size buffers with documented maximums, initialize pointers to NULL and check before use, and avoid dynamic allocation unless you implement deterministic pooling and clear ownership rules. When debugging, inspect memory regions with a debugger: check stack pointer, examine. data and. bss contents, and monitor heap usage if present. A common misconception is that C's unchecked arrays are safe if code 'usually' works; embedded systems demand rigorous checking because small mistakes can be catastrophic. Key takeaway: combine careful code patterns with runtime inspection to prevent and detect memory errors early.

keyIdea.title: Defensive habits
keyIdea.text: Use bounds checks, initialize pointers, and prefer static allocation; pair these with debugger inspection to catch errors early.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Common Memory Mistakes
Core Concept

Avoid these pitfalls

Cards list mistakes with prevention tips.

Buffer overflow
Always check bounds and prefer fixed-size buffers with clear limits.
Stack overflow
Avoid large local arrays and recursion. Move big buffers to static storage.
Uninitialized & dangling pointers
Initialize pointers to NULL and clear them after free; avoid returning addresses to stack-allocated memory.
Key Takeaway

Defensive coding and static allocation reduce the most common and dangerous memory errors in embedded systems.

Debugging cards
Use the debugger
  • Inspect addresses of globals, statics, and locals.
  • Monitor stack pointer in different contexts (main and interrupts).
  • Check for overwritten memory near array boundaries.
Check your understanding

Which is safer: a global static buffer or a large local buffer used in many places? Why?

screens.title: Practical Activity: Inspecting Variable Addresses
screens.subtitle: Declare globals, locals, and static counters and observe where they live

narration.text: A hands-on exercise anchors theory in practice. Create a program that declares a global array of 100 uint32_t values, a function that declares a local array of 10 values, and a static counter inside a function. Build and run the program under the debugger, break inside the function, and observe memory addresses. You should see the global array located in. data or. bss depending on initialization and the local array on the stack with an address near the current stack pointer. The static counter will have a persistent R A M address in. data or. bss but is only accessible by the function that defines it. This exercise demonstrates how lifetime and scope map to memory regions and helps you estimate sizes. When debugging, also watch the stack pointer across calls and interrupts to detect how much stack each function consumes. A common pitfall during this activity is expecting local addresses to remain the same across calls; their exact stack address changes with call depth. Key takeaway: debugging memory addresses makes the distinctions concrete and helps you make safe allocation choices for production code.

keyIdea.title: Activity insight
keyIdea.text: Inspecting addresses in a debugger solidifies understanding of where globals, locals, and statics live at runtime.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Inspecting Variable Addresses
Hands-on Activity

Declare and observe

A step checklist helps you run the experiment and what to expect in the debugger.

  1. Declare a global array of 100 uint32_t values.
  2. Write a function with a local array of 10 uint32_t and a static counter.
  3. Set a breakpoint inside the function and inspect addresses of the three variables.
  4. Observe which region each address belongs to and how the stack pointer changes across calls.
Key Takeaway

Use the debugger to validate your assumptions about variable placement and stack usage before deploying code.

Example code snippet
uint32_t g_array[100];

void func(void) {
  uint32_t local[10];
  static uint32_t counter = 0;
  counter++;
  // breakpoint here and inspect addresses
}
Misconception check

Don't assume stack addresses are stable; they depend on current call depth and saved state.

screens.title: Assessment: Why malloc is Discouraged
screens.subtitle: Explain risks and provide a safe alternative design

narration.text: A short assessment question helps solidify judgement about memory allocation choices. Ask: why is malloc generally discouraged in embedded bare-metal programming? The correct reasoning ties several facts together. First, heap fragmentation can make allocation unpredictable over time. Second, heap size on microcontrollers is often tiny, so leaks or excessive allocations quickly exhaust memory. Third, handling allocation failures adds complexity and failure modes that are hard to test in all conditions. Finally, many embedded systems must run unattended for long periods, so deterministic memory behavior is essential. A strong alternative is to use fixed-size buffers or a statically allocated pool that is allocated at startup and reused, which guarantees available memory and simplifies error handling. When answering, give a concrete alternative design: for variable-size incoming messages, preallocate a pool of maximal-sized buffers with a free list and take and return buffers deterministically. A common misconception is that avoiding malloc means poor memory efficiency; instead it trades some peak utilization for predictability and reliability. Key takeaway: prefer deterministic, static allocation strategies for systems that must be robust and long-lived. Assessment: Why malloc is Discouraged means explain heap risks and propose static allocation patterns like fixed pools as reliable alternatives.. In practical terms, explain risks and provide a safe alternative design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Design Guidelines for Reliable Memory Use
screens.subtitle: Practical rules to keep embedded programs predictable

narration.text: This final lesson slide distills practical rules you can apply immediately. First, prefer const for immutable data so it can stay in flash and not consume R A M. Second, avoid large automatic arrays; if you need big buffers, make them static or global with clear ownership. Third, keep functions shallow and small to limit stack growth, and avoid recursion on systems with limited stack. Fourth, if you must use dynamic memory, isolate it in a well-tested allocator with deterministic behavior and error handling. Fifth, measure stack usage during testing by filling stack memory with a pattern and observing the high-water mark. A concrete practice is to instrument startup to check the stack pointer against an expected limit and fail gracefully if exceeded. A common misconception is that small, occasional over-allocations are harmless; on embedded devices even rare overflows can cause difficult-to-reproduce failures. Key takeaway: apply these rules consistently and use debugging tools to validate assumptions about memory layout and usage during development and testing. Design Guidelines for Reliable Memory Use means prefer const and static buffers, keep stack usage small, and validate memory assumptions with tests and debugger inspections.. In practical terms, practical rules to keep embedded programs predictable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Engineering rules
keyIdea.text: Prefer const and static buffers, keep stack usage small, and validate memory assumptions with tests and debugger inspections.

Pro Tip

Rules for predictable memory

Prefer const in flash
Keep immutable data in flash to save RAM for runtime variables.
Use static pools
Preallocate buffers and reuse them to avoid heap fragmentation.
Limit stack depth
Keep functions shallow and avoid recursion to control stack growth.
Measure & validate
Use stack-fill tests and debugger inspections to find high-water marks and overflows.
Key Takeaway

Consistent rules and measurement make embedded memory behavior predictable and safe.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Summing up: the reset vector and startup code prepare the runtime environment for your program by initializing the stack and setting up global data. Memory regions have distinct roles:. text stores code in flash,. data holds initialized globals copied into R A M at startup,. bss contains zero-initialized storage, the stack holds local frames, and the heap is optional and risky on small systems. Variable storage classes map to these regions: globals and statics persist for the program lifetime, locals use stack space only during calls. Common errors include buffer and stack overflow, uninitialized and dangling pointers, and heap fragmentation. The practical rule is to favor static, fixed-size allocation patterns and to inspect memory with a debugger to validate assumptions. These ideas help you design embedded applications that are robust, deterministic, and easier to debug. Carry this checklist into your next project: initialize carefully, bound stack usage, avoid heap when possible, and validate with tools.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Startup + memory layout + disciplined allocation choices keep embedded systems reliable.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for everyday embedded development

narration.text: Keep three compact rules in mind: 1) Startup code sets the runtime stage — never assume main is first. 2) Memory regions are not interchangeable — place code and immutable data in flash, persistent variables in data or bss, and transient buffers on the stack with limits. 3) Avoid the heap unless you have a deterministic allocator — prefer static pools and fixed buffers for long-lived devices. These succinct guidelines will guide design choices for reliable firmware and help you prioritize where to invest testing and debugging effort. When you face a memory-related bug, inspect the reset sequence, verify. data and. bss contents, and examine the stack pointer to find the root cause. Carry these reminders into code reviews and design notes to keep systems predictable and maintainable. What to Remember means startup matters, memory regions have roles, and prefer static, deterministic allocation patterns.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for everyday embedded development. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Startup matters, memory regions have roles, and prefer static, deterministic allocation patterns.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › What to Remember
Startup first
Reset vector → startup code prepares stack and data before main.
Respect regions
Use flash for code/constants; use RAM where mutability is required.
Prefer static
Avoid heap fragmentation by using fixed pools and global buffers where appropriate.
Final takeaway

Make memory choices that keep your embedded system deterministic and testable throughout its lifetime.
